title: An Experimental Performance Evaluation of DC Power Generation and Power Loss in Full-Bridge Rectifier of Cantilever Type of Piezoelectric Vibration Energy Harvester

sections.heading: AN EXPERIMENTAL PERFORMANCE EVALUATION OF DC POWER GENERATION AND POWER LOSS IN FULL-BRIDGE RECTIFIER OF CANTILEVER TYPE OF PIEZOELECTRIC VIBRATION ENERGY HARVESTER
sections.text:
Kazuhiko ADACHI Department of Mechanical Engineering Kobe University Graduate School of Engineering 1-1Rokkodai-cho, Nada-ku, Kobe, Hyogo 657-8501 Japan kazuhiko@mech.kobe-u.ac.jp

sections.heading: ABSTRACT
sections.text:
Rotating machinery is widely used in the industrial plant. In order to ensure safety operation of the rotating machinery, vibration condition monitoring of the machinery can play a crucial role. Authors have proposed a cantilever type of vibration energy harvester for vibration condition monitoring applications of rotating machinery. Proposed energy harvester consisted of Macro-Fiber Composite (MFC).

In this study, not only the DC power generation performance but also power loss in full-wave bridge rectifier of the proposed vibration energy harvester is experimentally evaluated. The maximum DC output power through $2 8 7 . 6 ( \mathrm { k } \Omega )$ resistor which includes instruments internal resistances obtained $1 0 9 . 5 ( \mu \mathrm { W } )$ when subjected to vibration source input magnitude of $0 . 7 1 ( \mathrm { m m } / \mathrm { s } \ \mathrm { r m s } )$ at the resonant frequency of the harvester. The impedance matching between MFC actuators and the electrical resistive load was also effective for maximizing the DC power transfer of the vibration energy harvester. The power loss in full-wave bridge rectifier reached $1 3 . 7 ( \mu \mathrm { W } )$ at the resonant frequency.

sections.heading: INTRODUCTION
sections.text:
In recent years, various studies of cantilever types of piezoelectric vibration energy harvesters have been presented [1-7]. Figure 1 and Table 1 summarize the characteristics of these piezoelectric vibration energy harvesters whose vibration sources were several common indoor vibration sources except the industrial rotating machinery[8]. The maximum acceleration magnitudes of the vibrations and corresponding dominant frequencies at which the maximum output power occurred for several common indoor vibration sources are shown in [2]. In the vibration condition monitoring applications of rotating machinery, vibration sources should be considered from the practical vibration condition of the rotating machinery. ![](images/e163dc948ac2869f7d04003690aa0d81f6b84fccd6de61cc37a6d82af18af28a.jpg) Figure 1 Power generation performance of piezoelectric vibration energy harvester compared with regulation by ISO10816-1 [8]. In the previous authors' studies [8, 9], it was assumed that the typical casing vibration amplitude of the rotating machinery was 0.71 $\mathrm { ( m m / s ~ r m s ) }$ which is equal to the upper limit of Zone A for class I rotating machinery (ISO 10816-1 standard [10]). This vibration amplitude was the input vibration for experimental evaluation of the AC power generation performance of the prototype vibration energy harvesters in all frequency range. The generated AC power of the proposed energy harvester was measured through experiment when subjected to vibration source input magnitude of $0 . 7 1 ( \mathrm { m m / s }$ rms) at the resonant frequency of the harvester by using the electrodynamic shaker. The mechanical resonant frequency of the piezoelectric bimorph cantilever was tuned to the rotating speed of a typical 4-pole induction motor driven rotating machine. The maximum AC power, $1 5 1 . 8 ( \mu \mathrm { W } )$ ,was experimentally obtained with the electrical resistive load $1 0 9 . 7 ( \mathrm { k } \Omega )$ [9]. All experimental results indicated that the impedance matching between MFC actuators and the electrical resistive load was effective for maximizing the AC power transfer of the vibration energy harvester. In this study, not only the DC power generation performance but also the power loss in full-wave bridge rectifier of the proposed vibration energy harvester is experimentally evaluated.

sections.heading: Experimental Setup
sections.text: Figure 2 shows proposed vibration energy harvester of the cantilever type piezoelectric bimorph [8, 9]. The piezoelectric bimorph consisted of a pair of d31 type MFC actuators (Smart Materials Co., Part Number: M2814P2) [11] which were bonded on the surface of the substrate by two-part epoxy adhesive. The properties of vibration energy harvester are shown in Table 2. The middle substrate was a steel plate of 0.8 (mm) thickness. The mechanical resonant frequency of the cantilever was tuned about 26.3 $\left( \mathrm { H z } \right)$ by using tip mass shown in the figure. The resonant frequency was close to the normal operating speed of the 4-pole three-phase induction motor. In Table 2, the capacitance and the resistance of MFC were measured by impedance analyzer (HIOKI, Japan, LCR HiTESTER 3552) in series configuration at the frequency of $2 6 . 3 7 5 \mathrm { ( H z ) }$ .

sections.heading: DC Power Generation Evaluation
sections.text:
Figure 7 shows both experimentally evaluated AC and DC power generation performance with respect to electrical resistive load $R _ { D C }$ Experimental results show that the generated maximum effective AC power was $1 5 1 . 8 ( \mu \mathrm { W } )$ . The maximum effective AC power was obtained with the electrical resistive load $R _ { D C } = 1 0 9 . 7 ( \mathrm { k } \Omega )$ (the variable resistance $R _ { L } = 1 1 0 . 8 ( \mathrm { k } \Omega ) )$ at the excitation frequency $2 6 . 1 3 ( \mathrm { H z } )$ . On the other hand, the generated maximum effective DC power was $1 0 9 . 5 ( \mu \mathrm { W } )$ .The maximum effective DC power was obtained with the electrical resistive load $R _ { D C } = 2 8 7 . 6 ( { \mathrm { k } } \Omega )$ (the variable resistance $R _ { L } = $ $2 8 7 . 6 ( \mathrm { k } \Omega ) )$ at the excitation frequency $2 6 . 1 3 ( \mathrm { H z } )$ It indicates that the impedance matching between MFC actuators and the electrical resistive load was effective for maximizing the power transfer of the vibration energy harvester. However, the impedance matching conditions for each maximum power transfer were different from each other. ![](images/e11d0151cbfcea9966d754cc9ba5663f0175dd6bd15d088ca0cd1e1299653167.jpg) Figure 7 AC and DC power generation performance of the vibration energy harvester with respect to electrical resistance. ![](images/28a63981f67a8b22c01078a9e90e6f250f7ca305f3b9b6d6ef60c1bf3ff63bf1.jpg) Figure 8 Power conversion efficiency of the vibration energy harvester with respect to electrical resistance. Figure 8 shows the power conversion efficiency defined by $$ \eta = \left( \overline { { P } } _ { D C } / \overline { { P } } _ { A C } \right) \times 1 0 0 \left( ^ { \circ } \circ \right) , $$ for the vibration energy harvester with respect to electrical resistance. The maximum power conversion efficiency, $9 9 . 4 \%$ was obtained with the electrical resistive load $R _ { D C } = 3 4 0 . 8 ( { \mathrm { k } } \Omega )$ (the variable resistance $R _ { L } ~ = ~ 3 4 0 . 8 ( \mathrm { k } \Omega ) )$ at the excitation frequency $2 6 . 1 3 ( \mathrm { H z } )$ . Figure 9 shows the AC and DC power generation performance of the energy harvester with respect to excitation frequency. The maximum generated AC power of the energy harvester $\overline { { P } } _ { A C } \ : = \ : 1 5 5 . 8 ( \mu \mathrm { W } )$ was obtained when the excitation frequency was $2 6 . 1 ( \mathrm { H z } )$ with the electrical resistive load $R _ { D C } =$ $1 0 9 . 7 ( \mathrm { k } \Omega )$ (the variable resistance $R _ { L } ~ = ~ 1 1 0 . 8 ( \mathrm { k } \Omega ) )$ . The maximum generated DC power of the energy harvester $\begin{array} { l l } { { \overline { { P } } } _ { D C } } & { = } \end{array}$ $1 0 1 . 2 ( \mu \mathrm { W } )$ was obtained when the excitation frequency was $2 6 . 1 ( \mathrm { H z } )$ with the electrical resistive load $R _ { D C } = 1 4 9 . 7 ( \mathrm { k } \Omega )$ (the variable resistance $R _ { L } = 1 5 1 . 9 ( \mathrm { k } \Omega ) )$ . These results indicated that the exciting at the resonant frequency of the vibration energy harvester was effective for maximizing the power transfer of the vibration energy harvester. Consequently, it indicated that the variation of the excitation frequency could be estimated from the generated power. These experimental results showed that there was a possibility for self-sensing function. The vibration severity due to the unbalance vibration of the rotating machinery could be estimated by the generated AC or DC power of the vibration energy harvester. ![](images/c7413becd449da849b8f55510d58e2d290d824aef81ab31e8d2f56501cd9a8fd.jpg) Figure 9 AC and DC power generation performance of the vibration energy harvester with respect to excitation frequency. sections.heading: Power Loss in Full-Wave Bridge Rectifier
sections.text:
The power loss in full-wave bridge rectifier was estimated by $\overline { { P } } _ { A C } \mathrm { ~  ~ { ~ - ~ } ~ } \overline { { P } } _ { D C }$ using measured values. In the numerical analysis, the forward and reverse power losses, $P _ { f }$ and $P _ { r } ,$ were calculated in each period by using following equations, respectively.

$$
P _ { f } = I _ { f } \times V _ { f }
$$

where

$$
I _ { f } = \sqrt { \frac { 1 } { T } \int _ { 0 } ^ { T } { i _ { f } } ^ { 2 } d t }
$$

$$
{ \cal V } _ { f } = \sqrt { \frac { 1 } { T } { \int _ { 0 } ^ { T } { \nu _ { f } } ^ { 2 } d t } } \ .
$$

Similarly,

$$
P _ { r } = I _ { r } \times V _ { r }
$$

where

$$
I _ { r } = \sqrt { \frac { 1 } { T } \int _ { 0 } ^ { T } { i _ { r } } ^ { 2 } d t }
$$

$$
V _ { r } = \sqrt { \frac { 1 } { T } \int _ { 0 } ^ { T } { \nu _ { r } } ^ { 2 } d t } .
$$

Figure 10 shows both experimental and numerical estimated power loss in full-wave bridge rectifier. The power loss in the bridge rectifier depends on the electrical resistive load $R _ { D C }$ . The power loss in the bridge rectifier reached $1 3 . 7 ( \mu \mathrm { W } )$ when the maximum effective DC power was obtained with the electrical resistive load $R _ { D C } = 2 8 7 . 6 ( { \mathrm { k } } \Omega )$ (the variable resistance $R _ { L } ~ = ~ 2 8 7 . 6 ( \mathrm { k } \Omega ) )$ at the excitation frequency $2 6 . 1 3 ( \mathrm { H z } )$ . It indicates that the power loss in the bridge rectifier could not neglect in the proposed vibration energy harvester. Table 4 summarizes the experimental results.

sections.heading: CONCLUSIONS
sections.text: In this study, the DC power generation performance and the power loss in full-wave bridge rectifier of the proposed vibration energy harvester were experimentally evaluated. The maximum DC output power through $2 8 7 . 6 ( \mathrm { k } \Omega )$ resistor which includes instruments internal resistances obtained $1 0 9 . 5 ( \mu \mathrm { W } )$ when subjected to vibration source input magnitude of 0.71 $\left( \mathrm { m m / s \ r m s } \right)$ at the resonant frequency of the harvester. The impedance matching between MFC actuators and the electrical resistive load was also effective for maximizing the DC power transfer of the vibration energy harvester. The power loss in full-wave bridge rectifier reached $1 3 . 7 ( \mu \mathrm { W } )$ Thus, the power loss in the bridge rectifier could not neglect in the proposed vibration energy harvester.
